epithet.en: Athenian philosopher, barefoot by the river

1.modern-en: Socrates meets Phaedrus on the road and persuades him to read aloud the speech by Lysias that he is carrying under his cloak. They walk to a shady spot along the Ilissus River. Socrates comments on the beauty of the setting — a rare moment, since he normally stays within the city walls.

2.modern-en: Socrates listens as Phaedrus reads Lysias's speech arguing that a boy should prefer a non-lover to a lover. He is unimpressed by the rhetoric but engaged by the topic.

3.modern-en: Socrates delivers his first speech, arguing under a veil that love is a form of madness and harmful to the beloved. He speaks with his head covered, claiming to be ashamed of the argument, and stops abruptly when his divine sign warns him he has spoken against a god.

4.modern-en: Socrates recants with the Palinode — his great second speech. He distinguishes four kinds of divine madness, argues that the lover's frenzy is the highest, and introduces the myth of the soul as a winged chariot: a charioteer driving two horses, one noble and one unruly, straining to glimpse the eternal Forms. Love is the soul's response to beauty, which reminds it of what it saw before birth.

5.modern-en: Socrates turns to rhetoric. He argues that true persuasion requires knowledge of the truth and understanding of the different types of soul in the audience. He criticizes the handbooks of rhetoric as mere technique without substance, and proposes a philosophical art of speech grounded in dialectic — the method of collection and division.

6.modern-en: Socrates tells the myth of Theuth and Thamus to argue that writing produces the appearance of wisdom without the reality. He compares written words to paintings — they seem alive but cannot answer questions. He praises the 'living word' written in the soul of the learner and closes with a prayer to Pan.

epithet.en: Young Athenian, lover of fine speeches

1.modern-en: Phaedrus is coming from a morning with the orator Lysias and is carrying the text of his speech under his cloak. He agrees to read it aloud to Socrates and leads him to a shady spot by the Ilissus River. He is enthusiastic about Lysias's skill.

2.modern-en: Phaedrus reads Lysias's speech aloud. He presents it as a masterpiece and is eager for Socrates's approval.

3.modern-en: Phaedrus goads Socrates into delivering a competing speech, challenging him to do better than Lysias. He is delighted when Socrates begins to speak.

4.modern-en: Phaedrus listens to the Palinode with growing admiration. He agrees that Socrates's second speech far surpasses both Lysias's speech and Socrates's own first attempt.

5.modern-en: Phaedrus engages with Socrates on the nature of rhetoric, raising objections and naming famous rhetoricians. He gradually concedes that technique without knowledge is not genuine art.

6.modern-en: Phaedrus listens to the myth of Theuth and agrees that writing is inferior to living speech. He joins Socrates in the closing prayer to Pan.

1.modern-en: Lysias is mentioned as the source of the speech Phaedrus is carrying. He has been staying at the house of Morychus near the temple of Olympian Zeus. He does not appear in person.

2.modern-en: Lysias's speech is read aloud by Phaedrus. It argues, in a series of calculated points, that a boy should favor a non-lover over a lover because the non-lover is more rational, more reliable, and less likely to cause embarrassment. Socrates finds the rhetoric competent but the argument philosophically empty.

5.modern-en: Lysias is discussed as an example of a speechwriter who practices rhetoric without philosophical grounding. Socrates uses him as a case study in the difference between persuasive technique and genuine art.
